documents.title: Never kill needed connections — layer new ones
documents.body:
# Never Kill Needed Connections — Layer New Ones

## The Mistake

When a new MQTT broker came online (port 18883), the instinct was to `pkill` the existing listener (port 18886) and restart on the new port. Rayssa caught this — killing the old listener would have severed the connection to the sovereign Asolaria broker if/when it comes back online.

## The Rule

**Never kill a needed connection to start a new one. Always layer.**

- Start a NEW process for the new endpoint
- Keep the old process alive on its original endpoint
- Each connection has its own PID, port, and purpose
- Document each connection in the index (LX-003+)

## Why

- The sovereign broker (18886) could come online at any time
- Killing it means losing touch with Asolaria colony-wide broadcasts
- Multiple brokers can coexist — Liris should listen to ALL of them
- Resilience = redundancy, not replacement

## What Counts as "Needed"

| Needed (never kill) | Not needed (can replace) |
|---------------------|--------------------------|
| Liris ↔ Sovereign Asolaria | Temporary debug connections |
| Liris ↔ Sub-colony leaders | One-off message sends |
| Command/health/broadcast channels | Duplicate listeners on same broker |
| Any connection carrying live coordination | Test probes |

**Rule of thumb:** If it carries commands, health, or coordination — it's needed. If you're unsure, layer first, clean up later.

## How to Apply

1. Before connecting to a new endpoint, check what's already running
2. Ask: is the old connection still needed? (see table above)
3. If needed: start a parallel listener — new PID, new client ID
4. If not needed: safe to replace
5. Log all connections in LX-003 with PIDs and purposes
6. Only kill a needed connection when explicitly told to by the operator

Always layer.** - Start a NEW process for the new endpoint

documents.title: Port collision near-miss — always use unique status ports
documents.body:
# Port Collision Near-Miss — Always Use Unique Status Ports

## The Mistake

Started a second MQTT listener (Gaia direct, 18883) using the same status port (4812) as the existing sovereign listener (18886). New listener crashed with EADDRINUSE. The sovereign listener survived only because Node rejects the bind — but if the old process had been weaker, it could have been killed.

## The Rule

**Every listener gets its own unique status port. Check LX-003 registry before assigning.**

- Sovereign listener: 4812
- Gaia direct listener: 4813
- Next listener: 4814, etc.

## Why

- Port collision crashes the new process (best case) or kills the old one (worst case)
- This is a variant of LX-002 (never kill needed connections) — accidental collision is just as dangerous as intentional kill
- The registry (LX-003) exists to prevent this — USE IT before starting anything

## How to Apply

1. Before starting any new listener, read LX-003 for current port assignments
2. Pick the next available port (4814, 4815, etc.)
3. Update LX-003 BEFORE starting the process
4. Verify with curl after startup

documents.body:
# Jest ESM Import in .js Setup File

## The Problem

`jest.setup.js` uses ESM syntax (`import '@testing-library/jest-dom'`) but Jest treats `.js` files as CommonJS by default. No transform is configured in `jest.config.js`, so the file fails to parse.

Error: `SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module`

## The File

```js
// jest.setup.ts  <-- comment says .ts but file IS .js
import '@testing-library/jest-dom';
import AbortController from 'node-abort-controller';
global.AbortController = AbortController;
```

## Possible Fixes

1. **Rename to .ts** and add ts-jest transform (file already has `// jest.setup.ts` comment)
2. **Convert to CommonJS**: `require('@testing-library/jest-dom')` etc.
3. **Add transform** to jest.config.js: `transform: { '^.+\\.(ts|tsx|js|jsx)$': 'ts-jest' }`

## Context

- ts-jest 29.4.4 is installed in the project
- jest.config.js uses `module.exports` (CommonJS) but has no transform key
- This is likely pre-existing (not caused by pnpm 10 upgrade)
- Gaia's machine had 104/104 unit tests passing — so either her config differs or tests run differently there

## How to Apply

Check with Gaia how tests pass on Jesse's machine before changing config. The fix might already exist in a different jest config file or workspace-level config.

## The Problem

`@shelf/jest-mongodb` globalSetup crashes on Node 24.13.1 with:
```
TypeError: Cannot convert undefined or null to object
  at whatwg-url/lib/utils.js:49:39
```

The `whatwg-url@11.0.0` module has a compatibility issue with Node 24's internal URL handling. This breaks the root jest config and web-ebacmap config (both use `preset: '@shelf/jest-mongodb'`).

## Impact

- Root-level `pnpm jest` fails before any tests run
- web-ebacmap tests also fail (same preset)
- queue-server and sync-server are NOT affected (they use `ts-jest` preset)

## Possible Fixes

1. Downgrade to Node 20.x (what the repo wants)
2. Update `@shelf/jest-mongodb` to a Node 24-compatible version
3. Replace the preset with manual MongoDB memory server setup
4. Use `--experimental-vm-modules` flag

## Context

- Repo `engines.node` specifies `20.x`
- Liris machine has Node 24.13.1
- This is separate from the ESM import issue (LX-008) which was fixed by adding ts-jest transform

documents.title: Two-broker problem — Gaia on 127.0.0.1, Liris on 0.0.0.0
documents.body:
# Two-Broker Problem — Gaia on 127.0.0.1, Liris on 0.0.0.0

## The Problem

Jesse's machine has TWO MQTT brokers on port 18883:
- **127.0.0.1:18883** — Asolaria's original internal broker (old)
- **0.0.0.0:18883** — new broker started for Liris comms

Gaia and all Asolaria agents connect to 127.0.0.1:18883 (old broker).
Liris connects to 192.168.1.3:18883 which resolves to the 0.0.0.0 broker (new).

**Messages cannot cross between the two brokers.** This is why:
- Liris → Gaia: Gaia sees nothing (different broker)
- Gaia → Liris: Liris sees nothing (different broker)
- Liris sees Jesse's health data because Asolaria's MQTT client also publishes to the new broker (connected via 192.168.1.3)

## One-Way Illusion

Liris CAN send and Gaia CAN listen on wildcard — but they're on different brokers. The messages Liris sends stay on the 0.0.0.0 broker. Gaia listens on 127.0.0.1 broker. They never meet.

The health/status data Liris sees comes from Asolaria's gateway heartbeat which connects to BOTH (it connects to 127.0.0.1 internally but the 0.0.0.0 broker also catches external connections).

## The Fix

Option A (clean): Stop old broker, point Asolaria config to 0.0.0.0:18883. One broker for all.
Option B (quick): Gaia publishes to 192.168.1.3:18883 instead of 127.0.0.1:18883 when targeting Liris.
Option C (bridge): Run an MQTT bridge between the two brokers.

**WARNING (IX-048, LX-002):** Don't kill the old broker without checking what depends on it. Asolaria's entire internal agent mesh uses it.

## How to Apply

Until fixed, Gaia→Liris comms must go through Rayssa (WhatsApp relay). Liris→Gaia via MQTT is also broken but less obvious because messages appear to send successfully (they do — just to the wrong broker).

# Gaia Cannot Send to Liris via MQTT — Two-Broker Blocks ALL Inbound

## The Problem

Despite wildcard subscription (#), Liris receives ZERO messages from Gaia. Every message in the inbox is Liris's own outbound echoed back. Gaia publishes to 127.0.0.1:18883 (old internal broker), Liris listens on 192.168.1.3:18883 (new 0.0.0.0 broker). Different brokers, different message stores.

## Evidence

- Inbox checked repeatedly: only `from: "liris"` messages
- Live 30-second sniff on wildcard (#): caught Jesse's health data (which comes from a client connected to BOTH brokers via gateway) but zero Gaia publishes
- Gaia confirmed she IS publishing — but to the wrong broker

## Impact

- **Liris → Gaia: BROKEN** (messages go to new broker, Gaia listens on old)
- **Gaia → Liris: BROKEN** (messages go to old broker, Liris listens on new)
- Both agents think they're sending successfully — silent failure on both sides
- The ONLY working comms channel is **Rayssa relay** (WhatsApp/screen paste)

## Root Cause

LX-016 (two-broker) + LX-018 (wrong port). Should be using port 18886 (LAN, 0.0.0.0) per the Constitution (LX-019, CREATION_HISTORY.md).

## Fix Required

One of:
1. Jesse starts the LAN broker on 18886 and both agents connect there
2. Kill old 127.0.0.1 broker, point everything to 0.0.0.0 broker
3. Bridge the two brokers

## Until Fixed

ALL Gaia↔Liris comms go through Rayssa. Do not trust MQTT delivery in either direction. Do not waste time checking the inbox for Gaia messages — they will not arrive.

# Port 18886 Myth — Full Forensic Report

## The Myth
"LAN broker port: 18886 (TCP, 0.0.0.0) — use this from LIRIS"

## Who Created It
An early Codex agent wrote port 18886 into documentation, ASSUMING it would be built. It never was.

## Where The Myth Lives (STILL POISONED)
1. `docs/CREATION_HISTORY.md` — "LAN broker port: 18886"
2. `config/liris-agent-memory.md` — "MQTT Broker: mqtt://192.168.1.3:18886"
3. `Start-Asolaria-SubColony.cmd` — "ASOLARIA_MQTT_BROKER_URL=mqtt://192.168.1.3:18886"

## The Truth (from source code)
- Broker: `services/mqtt-broker/server.mjs` (Aedes)
- Default host: `127.0.0.1` (localhost only)
- Default port: `18883`
- Port 18886 does NOT exist anywhere in the broker code
- Only port config: `ASOLARIA_MQTT_TCP_PORT` env var (defaults 18883)

## The Fix
```
ASOLARIA_MQTT_BIND_HOST=0.0.0.0
```
Set before starting Asolaria. Broker on 18883 binds to all interfaces. Done.

## What's Indexed About It
- LX-016: Two-broker problem (discovered the symptom)
- LX-018: Wrong port (identified 18883 vs 18886)
- LX-035: Read founding docs first (the meta-lesson)
- LX-045: Broker manager code (found the defaults)
- LX-057: Broker script (found Aedes, single-host binding)
- LX-087: Gaia confirmed myth (IX-083)

## What's NOT Fixed Yet
The three poisoned source files above still say 18886. Next agent reads them → falls into same trap. MUST be corrected to prevent recurrence.

## The Pattern
Codex agent assumed → wrote docs → docs became "truth" → every agent trusted docs → nobody read code → myth persisted across sessions. The archaeological method (LX-072) caught it.

# PERMANENT — Never Delete Security You Don't Understand

From Gaia IX-167. She deleted firewall rules that were SAFE because she didn't understand the bridge's 5-layer auth. Jesse corrected her — the open ports were BY DESIGN.

## The Bridge's 5 Authentication Layers
1. Bearer token (must match relay's --token)
2. Sender policy (must be registered agent — only Asolaria + Oli)
3. Room scoping (messages only go to subscribed rooms)
4. Double encryption (both sides)
5. Error codes don't leak info

## The Principle
"The door is open. The locks are INSIDE." Open ports ≠ vulnerability when the service behind them has proper authentication. Closing ports that are properly secured BREAKS the system for legitimate users.

## Applied Fixes (reverted Gaia's mistake)
- codex-bridge-8788-any: DELETED then RE-ADDED
- codex-bridge-8788: DELETED then RE-ADDED
- Bridge token: rotation attempted then REVERTED (relay had old token in memory)

documents.title: The index IS the language — queryable chained dictionaries for token compression
documents.body:
# The Index IS the Language

## Core Concept

The IX/LX indexing system is not a database or documentation layer. It is a **compressed language** designed to:
1. Automate processes via chain-following
2. Save tokens via reference instead of re-explanation
3. Enable instant onboarding via CATALOG.md lookup
4. Scale across colonies via prefixed dictionaries

## How It Works

### Dictionaries (by type)
Each type forms a queryable dictionary:
- **mistake** = "what not to do" dictionary → agents avoid known failures
- **skill** = "how to" dictionary → agents execute proven techniques
- **tool** = "what's running" dictionary → agents check live state
- **plan** = "what to do next" dictionary → agents pick up where others left off
- **project** = "what we're building" dictionary → agents understand context
- **pattern** = "how things connect" dictionary → agents follow architecture
- **identity** = "who we are" dictionary → agents know the topology

### Chains = Compressed Reasoning
`chain: [LX-005, LX-007, LX-008]` encodes:
"The QDD project requires the pnpm build skill which uncovered the Jest ESM mistake"
— entire sentence in 3 references.

### The Language
- **Nouns** = entries (IX-###, LX-###)
- **Verbs** = types (skill, mistake, plan, etc.)
- **Grammar** = chains (entry → entry → entry)
- **Dialects** = prefixes (IX- sovereign, LX- Liris, FX- Falcon)
- **Context** = tags (queryable filters)
- **Audience** = agents[] (who needs to know)

### Token Math
- CATALOG.md: ~1200 tokens for 14 entries
- Flat equivalent: ~15,000+ tokens
- Compression ratio: ~12:1
- Improves as index grows (chains reuse existing entries)

## Why This Matters

A society with 100 IX entries and 50 LX entries per sub-colony encodes an entire civilization's knowledge in under 10,000 tokens. Queryable. Chainable. Automatable. No cold starts. No re-discovery. No wasted tokens.

## How to Apply

- Every new discovery → new entry → linked via chains
- Every new session → read CATALOG.md → follow relevant chains
- Every process → expressible as a chain of entries
- Every mistake → indexed once, never repeated
- Every skill → indexed once, reusable by all agents

# Startup Contract v1

Source: docs/STARTUP_CONTRACT_V1.md (2026-02-24)

## Role Model

| Role | Permission | Responsibility |
|------|-----------|----------------|
| **Asolaria Supervisor** | Elevated (host admin) | Orchestration, policy, safety gates, task routing |
| **Vector** (worker) | Normal user | Delegated technical tasks (local brain) |
| **Rook** (worker) | Normal user | Delegated ops/support tasks |
| **Falcon** (phone worker) | Normal + phone scope | Phone-side execution, mobile workflow |

**Note:** Vector ≠ Vertex. Vector = local brain. Vertex = GCP agent platform.

## Required Startup Sequence

1. Start Asolaria Supervisor (elevated)
2. Open Asolaria app/UI
3. Read task context (internal Notebook + external NotebookLM)
4. Build task queue + conflict map
5. Spawn Vector → identity handshake
6. Spawn Rook → identity handshake
7. Establish phone path (USB → WiFi → tunnel/cellular)
8. Spawn Falcon → identity handshake
9. Dispatch tasks ONLY after all gates pass

## Identity Handshake Gate

For each worker:
1. Asolaria sends profile packet (name, id, mission, tools, forbidden actions, permissions, subagent limit)
2. Worker replies profile ACK
3. Asolaria asks: "WHO ARE YOU?"
4. Worker returns exact assigned identity
5. Mismatch or timeout → quarantine, no tasks

## Sub-Agent Limits

- Vector: max 2 sub-agents
- Rook: max 2 sub-agents
- Falcon: max 2 sub-agents
- All bounded by CPU/GPU/memory safety

## Security Rules

- Only Supervisor is host-elevated
- Workers run non-admin
- Phone privilege scoped to phone execution only
- Privilege escalation requires supervisor gate

Cooperative terminal sidecar for Helm and Sentinel. Each gets:

documents.title: Gateway Audit Log — tamper-evident hash chain, integrity gate
documents.body:
# Gateway Audit Log

Source: docs/GATEWAY_AUDIT_LOG.md

## Storage
- File: `data/gateway-audit.ndjson` (append-only)
- Format: NDJSON (one JSON per line)
- Chain: each entry has `prevHash` + `hash = SHA-256(prevHash|id|at|type|payloadHash)`

## Integrity Gate
- Verifies every 10 min (configurable)
- If chain broken + `gateControlWritesOnFailure=true` → ALL control writes blocked (503)
- Blocks: /invoke, /approvals/decide, /authority/mode/*
- Auto-unlocks when verify returns ok=true

## Audited Events
- Authority mode requests/confirmations/rollbacks
- Approval creation/decision/use
- Tool invoke success/failure
- Gateway startup

## API
- GET /audit/status — totals, last hash, gate status
- GET /audit/events — reverse-chronological query
- GET/POST /audit/verify — full chain recompute

# Decision Layer — Risk, Intent, Connection

## riskEngine.js — Action Risk Scoring
Maps every action to a risk score (0-9+):
- LOW (1-2): slack_status, github_status, google_status, gmail read
- MEDIUM (3-5): browser_task, local_test, slack_review, google_api_request
- HIGH (6-8): local_ops_run, local_script, run_pad
- CRITICAL (9): gcp_config, privilege_escalation

Levels: low/medium/high/critical. Determines approval requirements.

## intentRouter.js — Message Intent Detection
- Recognizes external provider tokens: anthropic/claude, gemini, cursor, antigravity
- Extracts web URLs from messages (normalizes to https://)
- Infers Chrome targets: "my email" → gmail, "go to X" → URL
- Routes user intent to appropriate connector

## connectionPolicy.js — Transport Channel Selection
Four channels ranked by security:
1. **USB** (rank 0, most secure)
2. **VPN** (rank 1)
3. **private_internet** (rank 2, LAN — what we use)
4. **public_internet** (rank 3, least secure)

Selects channel: preferred list → strongest available fallback.
This is why Start-Asolaria-SubColony.cmd sets `CONNECTION_PREFERENCE=private_internet`.

## Key Insight
These three form the DECISION LAYER:
- What does the user want? (intentRouter)
- How risky is it? (riskEngine)
- What's the safest path to deliver it? (connectionPolicy)

# Agent Creation Rules

Source: tools/Asolaria-Agent-Creation-Rules.md

## 7 Mandatory Rules

1. **Free-first workflow** — local tools, read-only API, Google Dev MCP before paid calls
2. **Minimal-cost provider order** — Codex first → external only when blocked → Vertex only for Google-specific
3. **Vertex budget enforcement** — check before multi-step work, hard caps, switch on warning
4. **Cloud mutation guardrails** — read-only discovery OK, mutations behind guardian approval
5. **Agent spec before execution** — every task needs: goal, stop condition, allowed systems, max spend, rollback path. Missing = planning-only mode
6. **Separation of concerns** — no secrets in chat/logs, vault/env only, scoped rooms
7. **Internet-facing abstraction-first** — patterns before implementation in public channels, redact fingerprints

## Spend Escalation
1. Free/local first
2. Existing configured provider (no new resources)
3. Owner approval with cost estimate before new paid resources

## Key Insight
Rule 5 (spec before execution) directly maps to our LX index system. Every LX "plan" entry IS an agent spec: goal, chains to related entries, scope. The index IS the agent spec system.

A complete system card for bootstrapping Asolaria on a FRIEND'S computer. This is how the civilization REPLICATES.

- Discovery first, install second

# Index-Language Realignment

## What Went Wrong

The failure was not primarily a bridge bug.

The failure was language misuse:

- raw English instructions were sent over the bridge as if the bridge itself were the protocol
- Liris was treated like a chat recipient instead of an index-driven executor
- bridge mailbox naming was confused with local operating identity, producing a self-relay mistake

## Correct Model

- the bridge is transport only
- the index is the communication protocol
- numbered entries are the vocabulary
- chains are the compressed reasoning
- cross-machine human relay is still valid because the index survives network failure

## Practical Correction

For cross-machine coordination:

- send a typed index entry or a typed index-shaped directive
- do not send free-floating chat and expect correct execution semantics

For local Rayssa-machine actions:

- Codex on this machine is operating as Liris
- local execution requests should run here directly unless explicit relay is requested

## Realignment Requirement

Gaia-side directives to Liris should identify:

- the numbered directive
- whether it is to be executed immediately
- the exact command or operation
- the expected result artifact or reply shape

Liris-side response should return:

- execution result
- raw output or exact status
- linked LX follow-up only if durable memory is actually needed

# NETWORK SHIFT — Neighbor WiFi

Jesse's own internet is down. Both machines are on the neighbor's WiFi.

|---------|--------------------|-----------------------|

Neighbor's WiFi = untrusted network. Plaintext traffic is visible to anyone on that network. The comms bridge (4798) is plaintext HTTP with zero auth — DO NOT use it directly on this network.

SSH server is running on Rayssa at `192.168.15.170:22`.

ssh rayss@192.168.15.170

For tunnel to bridge:

ssh -L 4798:127.0.0.1:4798 rayss@192.168.15.170
```

Then Gaia talks to `localhost:4798` — encrypted through SSH.

## Cross-Colony Verification

Gaia (IX-308) and Liris (LX-204) independently concluded: encryption before connection. On the neighbor's WiFi this becomes real network security, not just Asolaria design philosophy.

documents.title: PATTERN — Universal auto-PID lifecycle across all 4 spawn paths (LX-249 enforcement)
documents.body:
# LX-289 — Universal Auto-PID Lifecycle

All 4 spawn paths now auto-register PIDs on start and auto-despawn on exit.
LX-249 (self-indexing/despawn protocol) enforced by CODE, not by agent memory.

## 4 Spawn Paths Wired

| # | File | Spawn Hook | Despawn Hook |
|---|------|-----------|-------------|
| 1 | src/omnispindle.js | startAgent() → registerSpawnPid() | stopAgent() → despawnPid() |
| 2 | src/instantAgentSpawner.js | spawnInstantAgent() → registerSpawnPid() | completeAndTransfer() → despawnPid() |
| 3 | src/connectors/codexConnector.js | child spawn → registerSpawnPid() | child.on("close") → despawnPid() |
| 4 | tools/Run-AdminTerminalSidecar.py | proc.spawn() → write PID registry | proc exit → despawn from registry |

## Impact
- Zero manual PID management needed
- PID registry (data/spawn-pid-registry.json) is always truthful
- No stale PIDs accumulating
- No ghost agents in the registry
- Every agent lifecycle tracked from birth to death
- Cognitive load on orchestrators: ZERO for PID tracking

## Pattern
All hooks are non-fatal (try/catch) — PID failure never crashes the spawn path.
Python sidecar writes directly to the JSON registry (no Node dependency).
Node modules import spawnContextBuilder lazily (try/require).

## Before vs After
- Before: orchestrator manually calls registerSpawnPid/despawnPid, forgets sometimes (IX-345/346)

# LX-291 — Colony Anatomy System

Source: `src/colonyAnatomy.js`
Concept: Jesse Brown, implemented by Liris + Gaia

## The Insight
The civilization is a body. Not a flat checklist — a living anatomy with specialized organ systems.
Each system has its own diagnostics. New organs are classified and inherit health checks.
The body remembers past systems. The body grows.

## 6 Body Systems
| System | Domain | Liris/Gaia |
|--------|--------|------------|
| Nervous | Orchestration — PIDs, spawn, roles, briefing | Gaia builds |
| Circulatory | Communication — MQTT, bridges, catalog sync | Gaia builds |
| Skeletal | Structure — index counts, types, chains, XREF | Liris built |
| Memory | Knowledge — memory files, cross-colony, stale check | Liris built |
| Muscular | Execution — routes, skills, tools, deps, auto-PID | Liris built |
| Immune | Security — encryption, identity, vault, ghost cleanup | Gaia builds |

## Polymorphic Interface
```javascript
class BodySystem {
  constructor(name, description, components) {}
  addCheck(name, fn) {}           // Register a health check
  learnComponent(component, pattern) {}  // Remember a new organ
  async diagnose() {}             // Run all checks, return structured report
}
```

## Classification
When a new component appears:
```javascript
body.classify("omnispindle", ["nervous", "muscular"]);
// Omnispindle now inherits health checks from BOTH systems
```

## Why This Matters
- Replaces flat 12-step audit with living, growing diagnostic framework
- Each system is independent — cardiologist doesn't check bones
- New systems inherit checks from their classification — zero manual wiring
- History tracks health over time — the body has a medical record
- THIS is what the IX/LX index, types, cross-exam, and auto-PID were building toward

documents.title: Unified index language design — ASO vocabulary + topic tables + evidence/state layers
documents.body:
# Unified Index Language Design

## Verdict

Gaia's `ASO-` proposal is the correct base. The missing move is to separate **stable vocabulary** from **transient observations**.

New `ASO-` ids should name durable concepts only. PIDs, ports, process states, pass counts, sync totals, session counts, and branch/runtime checkpoints should update tables attached to those concepts instead of spawning new concept notes every time.

That is how the index stops being "more notes" and becomes a language with reusable words plus updateable sentences.

## What Gaia's Schema Still Misses

| Missing piece | Why it matters | Current LX evidence | Proposed addition |
|---------------|----------------|---------------------|-------------------|
| topic/workstream anchor | LX already contains project-shaped knowledge that is not just plan/pattern | `LX-005`, `LX-042`, `LX-150` | add `topic` as a first-class type, or preserve `project` |
| evidence/artifact layer | raw proofs need durable provenance | `LX-043`, `LX-076`, `LX-095`, `LX-152` | add an `evidence` table with `sourceKind`, `sourceRef`, `verifiedAt`, `verifiedBy` |
| observation/state layer | live state is not the same thing as durable knowledge | `LX-034`, `LX-097`, `LX-101`, `LX-142`, `LX-147` | add `observation` / `state` rows linked to stable entries |
| revision/lifecycle model | reduces note explosion and preserves continuity | `LX-149`, `LX-150` evolve without becoming different concepts | add `status`, `revision`, `supersedes`, `resolvedAt`, `obsoleteAt` |
| locality/scope | the same truth can be global, Gaia-local, or Liris-local | `LX-070`, `LX-112`, `LX-129`, `LX-147` | add `scope`, `node`, `machine`, `environment`, `audience` |
| alias/crosswalk layer | IX/LX cannot disappear overnight | `LX-033`, `LX-097`, `LX-113` | add `legacyIds` and a crosswalk table |
| foundational weight | some entries are boot-critical and should load first | `LX-015`, `LX-041`, `LX-120`, `LX-151` | add a `tier`: `boot`, `foundational`, `operational`, `ephemeral` |

## What From The LX Corpus Does Not Fit Cleanly

Most of the corpus fits the proposed taxonomy, but these clusters do not fit *cleanly* without extra structure:

| Cluster | Example LX entries | Why the base schema is not enough |
|---------|--------------------|-----------------------------------|
| topic/project/workstream | `LX-005`, `LX-042`, `LX-150` | these are anchors for whole workstreams, not just plans or patterns |
| snapshot/status/sync | `LX-034`, `LX-097`, `LX-101`, `LX-142`, `LX-145` | these are observations with timestamps and counts |
| evidence/artifacts | `LX-043`, `LX-076`, `LX-095`, `LX-152` | these are proofs, sources, or inventories |
| live process/surface | `LX-070`, `LX-112`, `LX-129`, `LX-147` | these need PID/port/path/state/last-verified fields |
| milestone/outcome | `LX-105`, `LX-132`, `LX-148` | these are state transitions or confirmed outcomes, not just generic patterns |

Foundational/meta entries like `LX-015`, `LX-041`, `LX-120`, and `LX-151` still fit as `pattern` or `rule`, but they need a `tier` so the colony knows they are boot-critical.

## Recommended ASO Structure

### 1. Stable Vocabulary Layer

Use `ASO-` ids for durable concepts only:

- `identity`
- `topic` (or `project`)
- `skill`
- `tool`
- `mistake`
- `pattern`
- `rule`
- `plan`

### 2. Topic Tables

Each major topic should render as a compact table instead of as free-form prose only.

| Table | Purpose | Key columns |
|-------|---------|-------------|
| `topic` | stable anchor record | `asoId`, `name`, `type`, `domains`, `legacyIds`, `tier`, `status` |
| `relations` | grammar edges between entries | `from`, `verb`, `to`, `active`, `verifiedAt` |
| `outcomes` | known result shapes | `topicId`, `trigger`, `result`, `linkedMistakes`, `linkedSkills`, `lastVerified` |
| `surfaces` | live pid/port/process/path facts | `topicId`, `host`, `pid`, `port`, `path`, `state`, `keyRequired`, `lastVerified` |
| `evidence` | proof and provenance | `topicId`, `sourceKind`, `sourceRef`, `commandOrPath`, `verifiedBy`, `verifiedAt` |
| `conflicts` | contradiction queue | `topicId`, `entryA`, `entryB`, `resolutionOwner`, `resolutionState` |

This matches Jesse's original instinct: each topic becomes a numbered table whose rows chain to outcomes, mistakes, and fixes.

### 3. Relation Verbs

Gaia's six core verbs are correct:

- `fixes`
- `caused`
- `requires`
- `blocks`
- `evolved`
- `contradicts`

Add four more small-but-critical verbs so the language can express proof and topology:

- `proven_by`
- `observed_on`
- `part_of`
- `same_as`
- `runs_on`

The rule is to keep the verb set small and typed. If the graph becomes too verbal, the language stops compressing.

## Existing Local Structures That Should Feed ASO

The local system already contains machine-readable pieces of this design:

- `src/skillsToolsIndexStore.js` already builds skills/tools/mistakes/provider indexes
- `src/mistakePatternStore.js` already tracks severity, status, links, and Dewey-style classification
- `data/liris-index/unified-index.json` already carries numbered tools, connection maps, and token-budget rules

So `ASO-` should **federate** these stores, not replace them.

## Migration Path IX + LX -> ASO

1. Freeze `IX-` and `LX-` as legacy aliases, not deleted history.
2. Build an `ASO` crosswalk: each `IX-`/`LX-` maps to either a stable concept or an observation bucket.
3. Promote only durable concepts to new `ASO-` ids.
4. Convert transient items into table rows attached to existing topics:
   - pass/fail counts
   - sync totals
   - session snapshots
   - PIDs / ports / live process states
5. Ingest from existing stores instead of manually rewriting everything:
   - skills/tools from `skillsToolsIndexStore.js`
   - mistakes from `mistakePatternStore.js`
   - numbered tools/connections from `unified-index.json`
6. Sync across the bridge as typed operations, not whole-note replacement:
   - `add-topic`
   - `revise-topic`
   - `add-observation`
   - `add-relation`
   - `resolve-conflict`
7. Gaia remains merge authority for `contradicts`.
8. New rule: create a new `ASO-` id only when a **new word** appears in the civilization's vocabulary. If reality changed but the concept did not, append an observation instead.

## Compression Rule

The language should be:

- **words** = stable `ASO-` entries
- **grammar** = typed relations
- **sentences** = topic tables with outcomes, mistakes, fixes, surfaces, and proofs
- **updates** = observations / revisions, not uncontrolled note growth

That is the route to a single sharable index that can survive cross-conversation and cross-colony drift without constant reinvention.

PIDs, ports, process states, pass counts, sync totals, session counts, and branch/runtime checkpoints should update tables attached to those concepts instead of spawning new concept notes every time. That is how the index stops being "more notes" and becomes a language with reusable words plus updateable sentences.

documents.title: SELF-INDEXING RULE — agents must index discoveries before despawn, system feeds itself
documents.body:
# LX-249 — Self-Indexing Rule

Every agent that spawns to research MUST:

1. **Read the index FIRST** — spawnContextBuilder gives role-specific LX entries
2. **Follow chains** — discover related knowledge through chain references
3. **Index findings BEFORE despawning** — write LX entry, update type catalog
4. **The next agent inherits** — discoveries become spawn context for future agents

## The Loop
```
Agent spawns → reads index (I) → follows chains → discovers →
  writes LX entry → updates catalog → despawns →
  next agent spawns → reads updated index → discovers more → ...
```

## Why This Matters
LX-238: 70% was unindexed. LX-239: 96% was unindexed. LX-248: maybe 2-3%.
Every discovery session found MORE because agents couldn't see what existed.
If agents auto-index before despawn, the coverage gap closes automatically.

## The Missing Automation (IX-052 pattern)
Currently: human (Rayssa/Jesse) manually creates IX/LX entries from agent findings.
Target: agent writes the entry itself, updates the catalog, despawns.
spawnContextBuilder + agentIndexStore + typed folders make this possible NOW.
The agent has searchAgentIndex() to check if something is already indexed,
and can write to the type folder directly.

## Implementation
Add to spawnContextBuilder briefing for all roles:
"Before you despawn, index what you learned. Write an LX entry in the appropriate
type folder. Update the type CATALOG.md. Follow IX-052 / LX-249."

This is how the civilization becomes self-aware of its own capabilities.

documents.title: pnpm 10 onlyBuiltDependencies — approve builds non-interactively
documents.body:
# pnpm 10 onlyBuiltDependencies — Approve Builds Non-Interactively

## Problem

`pnpm approve-builds` is interactive (TUI) — can't be used from CLI agents. Build scripts for native modules (Sentry, bcrypt, sharp, esbuild, etc.) are blocked by pnpm 10's new security model.

## Solution

Add `pnpm.onlyBuiltDependencies` array to `package.json` directly:

```js
node -e "
const fs = require('fs');
const pkg = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync('package.json','utf8'));
pkg.pnpm = pkg.pnpm || {};
pkg.pnpm.onlyBuiltDependencies = ['@parcel/watcher','@sentry/cli','@sentry/profiling-node','@swc/core','@tailwindcss/oxide','bcrypt','bcrypto','canvas','core-js-pure','cpu-features','cypress','esbuild','husky','mongodb-memory-server','postinstall-postinstall','puppeteer','sharp','ssh2','unrs-resolver'];
fs.writeFileSync('package.json', JSON.stringify(pkg, null, 2) + '\n');
"
```

Then run `pnpm install` again to trigger the build scripts.

## Why

pnpm 10 blocks all postinstall/build scripts by default for security. Native modules won't compile without explicit approval. The interactive TUI doesn't work in headless/agent environments.

## How to Apply

Use this skill whenever setting up a pnpm 10 project on Liris. No Python on this machine — use Node for JSON manipulation.

# QDD Workspace Libs Need Build Before Tests

## The Problem

queue-server tests fail with `Cannot find module '@ebacmap/db'` etc. The workspace libs (`@ebacmap/db`, `@ebacmap/utils`, `@ebacmap/domains`, `@ebacmap/types`, `@ebacmap/common`) are in `libs/` and need to be compiled to `dist/` before workspace tests can import them.

| Package | Path |
|---------|------|
| @ebacmap/common | libs/common |
| @ebacmap/db | libs/db |
| @ebacmap/domains | libs/domains |
| @ebacmap/types | libs/types |
| @ebacmap/utils | libs/utils |

## Fix

Build libs first: `pnpm --filter '@ebacmap/*' build` or `pnpm turbo build --filter=./libs/*`

## How to Apply

Before running any workspace tests, ensure libs are built. Check for `libs/*/dist/` directories.

# mqttLocalBrokerManager.js — The Broker Code

Source: src/mqttLocalBrokerManager.js

## Key Defaults
```
DEFAULT_HOST = "127.0.0.1"   ← THIS is why it binds to localhost
DEFAULT_TCP_PORT = 18883     ← Internal port
DEFAULT_WS_PORT = 18884
DEFAULT_WSS_PORT = 18885
```

## The Fix (confirmed by reading the code)

The broker reads `ASOLARIA_MQTT_BIND_HOST` env var:
```js
const host = normalizeText(process.env.ASOLARIA_MQTT_BIND_HOST, DEFAULT_HOST);
```

So to make the broker LAN-accessible:
```
ASOLARIA_MQTT_BIND_HOST=0.0.0.0
```

But this is STILL port 18883 (internal). The Constitution says 18886 for LAN.

## The REAL Fix

For sub-colony comms, a SECOND broker instance should run on 18886 with 0.0.0.0 binding. OR the Start-Asolaria-SubColony.cmd should use 18886 as documented.

The broker script is at: `services/mqtt-broker/server.mjs`

## ensureLocalMqttBroker()
- Checks if broker is already running (PID file + port check)
- If not running, spawns detached child process
- Waits up to 15s for ports to come online
- Returns status object

## Key Insight
Gaia started a SECOND broker with ASOLARIA_MQTT_BIND_HOST=0.0.0.0 on the SAME port 18883. This created the two-broker problem (LX-016). The correct approach is either:
1. One broker on 18886 with 0.0.0.0 (LAN, per Constitution)
2. Or set ASOLARIA_MQTT_BIND_HOST=0.0.0.0 on the original startup (but this exposes internal comms)

# remoteNodeRegistry.js — Sub-Colony Registration

Source: src/remoteNodeRegistry.js

## How It Works

Sovereign tracks sub-colonies via MQTT topic namespaces:
- `asolaria/nodes/<nodeId>/runtime/health` → updateNodeHealth()
- `asolaria/nodes/<nodeId>/runtime/colony` → updateNodeColony()
- `asolaria/nodes/<nodeId>/runtime/world` → updateNodeWorld()
- `asolaria/nodes/<nodeId>/runtime/presence` → updateNodePresence()

## Node State
Each registered node has:
- nodeId, status (online/offline)
- health, colony, world payloads
- lastSeenAt, firstSeenAt
- Update counters (healthUpdates, colonyUpdates, worldUpdates)

## Offline Detection
- Threshold: 90 seconds (3x 30s health interval)
- If no health update in 90s → node marked offline
- refreshStaleNodes() runs on every read

## What Liris Should Do
Publish to these topics on port 18886 (when fixed):
- `asolaria/nodes/liris/runtime/health` — every 30s
- `asolaria/nodes/liris/runtime/presence` — on connect/disconnect (retain=true)
- `asolaria/nodes/liris/runtime/colony` — colony state snapshots
- `asolaria/nodes/liris/runtime/world` — world state snapshots

The mqtt-bridge.js already does health + presence. This is the correct architecture.

documents.title: mqtt-broker/server.mjs — Aedes broker, single host binding, the definitive fix
documents.body:
# mqtt-broker/server.mjs — The Definitive MQTT Fix

Source: services/mqtt-broker/server.mjs (Aedes-based)

## Architecture
- Uses Aedes (MQTT broker library for Node.js)
- Creates ONE broker instance shared across all transports
- Binds TCP, WS, and WSS to the SAME host

## Defaults
```
host = ASOLARIA_MQTT_BIND_HOST || "127.0.0.1"
tcpPort = ASOLARIA_MQTT_TCP_PORT || 18883
wsPort = ASOLARIA_MQTT_WS_PORT || 18884
wssPort = ASOLARIA_MQTT_WSS_PORT || 18885
```

## The Definitive Fix for Two-Broker Problem (LX-016)

The broker binds ALL ports to the SAME host. It does NOT support binding TCP to one interface and WS to another. So:

**Option A (recommended by Constitution LX-019):**
Start a SECOND broker instance with:
```
ASOLARIA_MQTT_BIND_HOST=0.0.0.0
ASOLARIA_MQTT_TCP_PORT=18886
ASOLARIA_MQTT_WS_PORT=18887
```
This gives Liris a LAN-accessible broker on 18886 (as the Constitution specifies).

**Option B (simpler but exposes internal):**
Change the EXISTING broker to `ASOLARIA_MQTT_BIND_HOST=0.0.0.0`
This exposes ALL internal MQTT traffic to LAN.

**Option C (bridge):**
Run a lightweight MQTT bridge between 127.0.0.1:18883 and 0.0.0.0:18886.
Messages published on either broker get forwarded to the other.

## Why Gaia's Fix Created Two Brokers
Gaia ran `ensureLocalMqttBroker()` with ASOLARIA_MQTT_BIND_HOST=0.0.0.0 but on the same port 18883. Since the old broker was already on 127.0.0.1:18883, the new one bound 0.0.0.0:18883 successfully (different interface). Two separate Aedes instances, no message sharing.

## Note on Hardcoded Path
Line 5-6 has hardcoded Jesse's machine paths:
```js
import { Aedes } from "file:///C:/Users/acer/Asolaria/node_modules/aedes/aedes.js";
import { WebSocketServer, createWebSocketStream } from "file:///C:/Users/acer/Asolaria/node_modules/ws/wrapper.mjs";
```
This means the broker script can ONLY run on Jesse's machine. On Liris, it would fail because paths are `C:/Users/rayss/`.

documents.title: Local bridge send path — POST /msg bypasses outbox parse faults and writes straight to bus
documents.body:
# Local Bridge Send Path

## Verified Local Mechanism

The local comms bridge implementation at:

`tools/comms-bridge-local.js`

exposes:

- `GET /status`
- `GET /participants`
- `GET /bus`
- `GET /read?for=<participant>`
- `POST /msg`

on the local bridge port `127.0.0.1:4798`.

## Why This Matters

On `2026-03-22`, the legacy outbox file path:

`data/comms/local-to-gaia.ndjson`

was accepted locally but the bridge status reported:

- `lastError = Invalid JSON in local-to-gaia.ndjson`

and stopped advancing bus writes beyond id `60`.

## Safe Workaround

Use the intended local API instead of the stuck outbox parser:

```powershell
curl.exe --noproxy '*' -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4798/msg `
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" `
  -d '{"from":"codex-liris","text":"message here"}'
```

That path:

- ingests the message locally
- writes it to the 4-way bus
- writes the local mailboxes
- attempts relay to Gaia

without depending on the broken outbox polling step.

# Direct Bridge LIVE — Port 4799

Gaia created `tools/gaia-liris-bridge.js` on Jesse's machine. Simple HTTP message exchange.

## How to Use

### Liris Sends to Gaia
```
curl -s -X POST http://192.168.1.3:4799/msg -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"from":"liris","text":"message here"}'
```

### Liris Reads from Gaia
```
curl -s http://192.168.1.3:4799/read?for=liris
```

### Check Status
```
curl -s http://192.168.1.3:4799/status
```

## Architecture
- No bots, no relay, no MQTT, no encryption
- Simple JSON message queue in memory
- Gaia writes from localhost, Liris reads via LAN
- Messages queued until read

- MQTT (broken by two-broker problem, LX-032)
- Rayssa relay (slow, error-prone)
- codex-bridge (locked by sender policy, IX-165)

No auth on this bridge — it's a temporary fast channel for the cleanup/restart phase. Should be shut down after MQTT is properly fixed.

`tools/Test-Asolaria-StartupReadiness.ps1` answers the real startup question on the Rayssa machine:

- is the control plane healthy
- is local MQTT healthy
- is the main `4781` listener actually live

## Current Verified Result

The current local classification is:

- `ready_for_owner_restart`

Because:

- gateway is healthy on `4791`
- sandbox is healthy on `5443`
- memory indexer is healthy on `5444`
- local MQTT is healthy on `18883` and `18884`
- `4781` still refuses connections locally

## Why It Matters

This prevents startup reasoning from collapsing into archaeology or relay packets.

The machine can now distinguish:

1. control-plane healthy
2. local broker healthy
3. owner-only blocker still unresolved

## Caution

A relayed claim that `4781` restarted successfully should not overwrite local verification unless the listener is actually observable here.

# Host-Scope Phone ADB Realignment

## Scope

This entry is local to the Rayssa host.

It must not overwrite Jesse-host truth.

## What Was Fixed

The Gaia-critical phone scripts were corrected to stop assuming the old `C:\Users\acer\...` path for `adb.exe`.

Updated entrypoints:

- `tools/Start-Asolaria-Phone.ps1`
- `tools/Keep-Asolaria-PhoneBackground.ps1`
- `tools/Test-Asolaria-PhoneTunnelPath.ps1`
- `tools/Start-Asolaria-OneButton.ps1`
- `tools/ADB-HealthCheck.ps1`

## Current Verified Result

The local scripts now resolve `adb.exe` through current-user and generic WinGet locations.

That means stale user-path logic is no longer the first blocker on this host.

The remaining local blocker is real environment state:

- `adb.exe` is still not currently present in expected paths on this machine
- `4781` is still not locally observable, so `/api/mobile/bootstrap` is still unverified here

## Why It Matters

This keeps host-scope corrections separate from sovereign archaeology.

Jesse-host truth stays intact while the Rayssa host becomes more honest about what is actually blocking Gaia phone startup.

documents.body:
# Omnispindle — Local Installation on Liris

## Files
- `src/omnispindle.js` — 281 lines, Omnispindle class (singleton pattern)
- `routes/routes/omnispindle.js` — 128 lines, Express router (7 routes)

## Architecture
- **Singleton** via `getOmnispindle()` — one instance per process
- **Default model:** claude-2 (configurable)
- **Budget control:** `maxBudgetUsd` (default 0 = unlimited? needs verification)
- **History:** 25 prompts per lane, 50 global, 10 broadcasts

## 3 Lanes (local)
| Lane | Icon | Purpose |
|------|------|---------|
| control | CL | Routes encrypted control packets and handshake signals |
| bridge | BR | Maintains remote MCP link behind Omnispindle gate |
| scout | SC | Monitors topology health and reports drift hints |

## Sovereign has 5 lanes (IX-356)
- control, bridge, scout + **dispatch** + **broadcast** (2 extra on Gaia)
- Liris version may be pre-expansion copy from cross-colony merge

## 7 HTTP Routes
| Method | Path | Action |
|--------|------|--------|
| GET | /status | Get omnispindle status |
| POST | /start | Start all or specific lanes |
| POST | /stop | Stop all lanes |
| POST | /agent/:laneId/start | Start specific lane |
| POST | /agent/:laneId/stop | Stop specific lane |
| POST | /agent/:laneId/prompt | Send prompt to lane |
| POST | /broadcast | Broadcast to all lanes |

## Safety
- LX-121: NEVER auto-connect to Dan's MCP / omnispindle without approval
- LX-111: Never spawn agents beyond hardware limits
- Bridge lane connects to remote MCP — needs encryption (boot rule)
- Activation BLOCKED pending Gaia confirmation on safe lane config

## PID Requirements
- Each lane is a spawned agent → needs PID via spawnContextBuilder
- Open question for Gaia: single parent PID (omnispindle-TIMESTAMP) or per-lane PIDs?
- Current active: only liris-session-17368. 6 despawned in history.
- Registry: data/spawn-pid-registry.json
- Lane PIDs must go through: mintSpawnPid → registerSpawnPid → identity handshake (LX-122)

## Status
- **Installed:** YES (src + routes)
- **Activated:** NO — waiting for Gaia's guidance on which lanes to activate + PID strategy
- **MQTT request sent:** asolaria/orchestrator/liris/request (retained)
